Flagship project:
- Shoot the Moon: A 3D lunar strategy game built for phone browsers. Land, mine, build, strike, survive the counterattack and defend your claim on the Moon.
  Status: Feature freeze
  Key facts: 576 unit tests; 24 Playwright spec files; React + TypeScript + Three.js
  Proof: Ambitious 3D browser work can be built with real test coverage behind it.
  Hard part: Keeping player saves compatible while the game kept growing. The save schema is at v9, with migration support for saves from v1 through v8.
  How it was built: React 19, TypeScript, Three.js and React Three Fiber on Vite. The game uses zero external 3D model files and two NASA lunar textures. Verification: 576 unit tests across 63 files and 24 Playwright spec files.
  Tags: React 19, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Vite, NASA lunar textures
  Visual artifacts: /media/shoot-the-moon/poster-1280.jpg
  Reel: /media/shoot-the-moon/reel-57s-1080.mp4
  Live: Play Shoot the Moon (https://shootthemoon.pages.dev/)
  Source: View Shoot the Moon source (https://github.com/mataindustries/shootthemoon)
  Case study: Shoot the Moon case study (https://ziggurat.pages.dev/work/shoot-the-moon/)

Major project:
- PermitPulse: Cited parcel research for Los Angeles properties. Every finding in a brief is labeled Supported, Conflict or Unknown, tied to its official source and reviewed by a person.
  Status: Introductory offer live
  Current status: $149 per property, or three properties for $299, City of Los Angeles first. Briefs are delivered within 48 business hours after scope and payment are confirmed.
  Key facts: Every finding cited; Unknown stays unknown; Reviewed by a person
  Proof: A software and data experiment can become a disciplined research workflow, real-property proof, and paid-service offer.
  Hard part: Jurisdiction records arrived with inconsistent structure, incomplete ownership signals, stale portal states, and chronology that had to be reconstructed rather than assumed.
  How it was built: AI assists with organizing and reviewing case material, implementation passes, and quality checks. It never approves evidence or acts as an autonomous permit reviewer; findings and delivery require human approval. Briefs preserve source limits and unknowns and do not make legal, title, architectural, engineering, entitlement, code-compliance, or government determinations.
  Tags: Civic operations, Evidence provenance, Reviewer workflow, Cloudflare infrastructure, Private storage, Deterministic rendering
  Visual artifacts: /projects/permitpulse/permitpulse-parcel-brief-1500.webp, /projects/permitpulse/permitpulse-01-mission-control.png, /projects/permitpulse/permitpulse-02-evidence-register.png, /projects/permitpulse/permitpulse-03-case-timeline.png, /projects/permitpulse/permitpulse-04-packet-preview.png, /projects/permitpulse/permitpulse-05-review-packet-cover.png, /projects/permitpulse/permitpulse-06-executive-summary.png, /projects/permitpulse/permitpulse-07-dependency-map.png, /projects/permitpulse/permitpulse-08-supporting-evidence.png
  Operational flow: Research public sources → Separate certainty → Human review → Deliver concise brief
  Milestones: Primary and public-source research; Facts, inference, conflicts, and unknowns separated; Anonymized real-property proof; Human-reviewed briefs; Decision-ready output; Live introductory offer
  Engineering: React and TypeScript shape the operational interface. Cloudflare Workers run the application edge, D1 holds structured case state, R2 keeps evidence private, and Better Auth protects the workspace. The packet engine produces consistent HTML and PDF deliverables from reviewed records.
  Technologies: React, TypeScript, Cloudflare Workers, Cloudflare D1, Cloudflare R2, Better Auth, Deterministic rendering, PDF generation, AI-assisted review, Human approval
  Live: Visit PermitPulse (https://getpermitpulse.com)

Supporting projects:
- SGVTurf: Connects local homeowner search intent to city guidance, official-source rebate context, a structured project brief, and relevant contractor discovery.
  Status: Live market test
  Current status: The homeowner brief, 2026 turf-replacement rebate resource, city guides, and editorial system are live. Founding-contractor outreach is testing the referral side.
  Proof: Useful local information can form a clear acquisition path from search intent to a contractor-ready inquiry.
  Hard part: Rebate rules change, city context varies, and an empty contractor roster must not look like participation.
  How it was built: AI assists with research organization, city-page implementation, funnel iteration, and outreach preparation. Rebate claims are checked against official sources. The founding test is explicit about its limits: no contractor participation, lead volume, revenue, or result is claimed.
  Tags: San Gabriel Valley, Local acquisition, Official-source research, Editorial systems, Contractor discovery
  Visual artifacts: /projects/sgvturf.webp
  Operational flow: Local search intent → Planning + rebate context → Structured project brief → Contractor discovery
  Live: Visit SGVTurf (https://sgvturf.com)
- Snapshot Studio: A lightweight sales tool for turning local visibility problems into fast visual reports and improvement plans.
  Status: Live sample tool
  Proof: Small businesses can receive fast, visual snapshots of search visibility problems and practical improvement plans.
  Hard part: The offer started too broad, outreach responses were inconsistent, and report value had to be made obvious faster.
  How it was built: AI supports prospect research, report drafting, local search framing, landing-page passes, and a repeatable audit structure. The human work is closing the gap between a useful audit and a paid offer.
  Visual artifacts: /projects/snapshot-studio.jpg
  Live: Open live sample (https://snapshot-studio.pages.dev)
- Xibalba Pinball: A mythic five-ball score attack with touch controls, browser physics, and a global Wall of Champions.
  Status: Live game
  Proof: AI-assisted development can ship a weird, playable, visually distinctive browser game.
  Hard part: Table tuning fought the art direction, collisions misbehaved, and several visual passes missed the intended underworld mood.
  How it was built: Built with AI support for physics implementation, Phaser iteration, asset direction prompts, debugging loops, and mobile polish. Table feel, collision edge cases, and taste decisions were earned through failed passes.
  Visual artifacts: /projects/xibalba.jpg
  Live: Play live (https://xibalba.pages.dev)
- BounceBox: A mobile-first physics groovebox that turns bouncing balls and AI-generated MIDI patterns into a playable instrument.
  Status: Live instrument
  Proof: Browser-native physics, audio, generative controls, and mobile UI can become a distinctive playable instrument.
  Hard part: Rhythm feel, touch ergonomics, MIDI prompt boundaries, and dense performance controls all had to be tuned into something playable.
  How it was built: TypeScript iteration with a custom ChatGPT MIDI Lab for generative pattern design, plus mobile UI passes, control naming, and performance-state testing. The taste work was making unusual mechanics feel intentional.
  Visual artifacts: /images/bouncebox/bouncebox-808-performance.png
  Live: Open live instrument (https://bouncebox.pages.dev)

Lab:
- Danger Close: A tactical browser survival game about piloting a salvage drone through dead zones, collecting resources, surviving enemy pressure, and upgrading hardware between runs.
  Status: Live game
  Current status: Live playable prototype
  Proof: AI-assisted development can ship a polished browser game loop with sector selection, upgrade systems, enemy pressure, resource collection, survival pacing, and premium sci-fi interface design.
  Hard part: Early balancing passes created uneven pressure, dense combat states reduced clarity, and experimental systems did not always share a clean plan.
  How it was built: Used Codex and frontier AI models for gameplay systems, UI polish, enemy behavior, upgrade design, copy, testing checklists, and rapid iteration. Balancing is still evolving and visual density needs tuning.
  Tags: Browser game, Survival loop, Drone combat, Upgrade systems, AI-assisted game design, Cloudflare Pages, Playable prototype
  Visual artifacts: /projects/danger-close.jpg, /projects/danger-close-sector.jpg, /projects/danger-close-upgrades.jpg, /projects/danger-close-combat.jpg
  Live: Play live (https://dangerclose.pages.dev)
- The Angeles Crest: An unofficial AC100 guide covering training, course strategy, crew logistics, qualifiers, gear, and local San Gabriel knowledge.
  Status: Public draft
  Proof: Research, editorial structure, local context, and frontend implementation can become a useful niche information system.
  Hard part: A broad brand concept had to narrow into one useful editorial resource with clearer reader intent.
  How it was built: AI supports research organization, editorial structure, site implementation, visual direction, and deployment. The project evolved in public, changed direction, and still carries the limits of an unofficial guide.
  Visual artifacts: /projects/angeles-crest.jpg
  Live: Open public draft (https://theangelescrest.pages.dev)

How I build with AI:
1. Find the real problem: Start with the workflow, constraint or failure that is actually costing someone time.
2. Specify the behavior: Define what should happen, what must not change and how success will be tested.
3. Use the right model for the job: Give coding agents narrow, testable work instead of asking one model to own the whole product.
4. Verify before it ships: Run the tests, inspect the output and keep the evidence.
Evidence: Shoot the Moon reached 576 passing unit tests before feature freeze.
